tasks.locator: Results > Subjective effects, 1st paragraph (p. 399, right column, continuing p. 400); Figure 1 (p. 400)
tasks.extracted: In a 15-day residential study of 7 volunteers given oral methamphetamine 10 mg twice a day on days 4-6 and 10-12 (5 mg twice a day in the other block), ratings of 'good drug effect' (F(1,48)=8.0) and 'high' (F(1,48)=15.0) were raised above the matched placebo baseline day only on the first day of the larger dose and had returned to baseline by day 3; the smaller dose did not differ from baseline on either rating. The two printed P values are transposed relative to their F values (editors' calculation).

tasks.locator: Results > Subjective effects, 2nd paragraph and Table 1 (p. 400); Results > Sleep (p. 401, right column)
tasks.extracted: Over the same three days the unwanted effects went the other way: dizziness (F=9.8) and flu-like symptoms (F=13.2) rose on day 3 but not day 1, and being unable to concentrate, chills, confusion, depression, nausea and 'bad drug effect' (F=17.4) became significant only on day 3, while 'heart pounding' and 'trouble sleeping' were raised on all three days. Sleep was disrupted on the first night only (total sleep time F=12.5, non-REM F=8.2, sleep efficiency F=8.1, movements F=15.4), which the authors also read as tolerance; there was no rebound on the placebo days after.

tasks.locator: Results > Food intake, 1st paragraph and the sentence at the top of the right column; Figure 3
tasks.extracted: The fall in food intake did not lessen across the three days: total daily intake was about 1150 kcal lower at 5 mg twice daily and about 1450 kcal lower at 10 mg twice daily than the placebo baseline on each of days 1, 2 and 3 (F(1,48)=19.2, 44.4 and 29.9; 62.7, 43.9 and 39.6; all P<0.0001), and intake was still below baseline on the first placebo day after each block.

tasks.locator: Results > Cardiovascular effects, continuing on p. 357 above the Discussion; Figure 3 (p. 357)
tasks.extracted: In 6 men who took 10 mg of slow-release oral methamphetamine daily for 13 days, the rise in heart rate over baseline after a fixed oral challenge dose (0.125 mg/kg) was significantly smaller on day 15 than on day 1 (F=8.26, P<0.03 in the Results and P<=0.035 in the summary, which is the value the F statistic gives). The day-1 and day-15 rises themselves are shown only as bars in Figure 3 and are not printed. There was no placebo challenge and no blinding, so habituation to a repeated procedure is not excluded.

tasks.locator: Results > Subjective effects (p. 355); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 357)
tasks.extracted: In the same men, peak ratings of 'high' after the challenge did not differ significantly between day 1 and day 15 (16.8, SEM 6.5, against 10.0, SEM 3.9, out of 100), and the authors state that this small response, under a fifth of the scale, limited the chance of observing tolerance to the subjective effect; peak blood-pressure rises were likewise too small (under 15 mm Hg systolic and 6 mm Hg diastolic) for tolerance to those effects to be tested.

tasks.locator: Results > Pharmacokinetic Analysis, last paragraph (p. 859, continuing p. 860); Table 2 (p. 861)
tasks.extracted: In the pharmacokinetic arm of the same 13-day regimen (8 men, challenge doses of 0.125 and 0.250 mg/kg), absorption, apparent clearance, renal clearance, the elimination rate constant and the half-life were unchanged between day 1 and day 15; the only significant changes were upward (peak concentration about 12.5% higher at the larger challenge dose). The printed power analysis shows a 20% change would have been detected for the elimination rate constant (detectable difference 21.2% and 14.8%), peak concentration (18.3% and 6.1%) and exposure (20.1% and 15.6%), so the fading response is not explained by faster clearance.

tasks.locator: Results > Tolerance > Cardiovascular and BAL effects; Figure 4 (left panel)
tasks.extracted: In 9 men given oral methamphetamine 10 mg three times over about 36 hours in a residential laboratory, alone or with alcohol, the heart-rate area under the curve was significantly smaller at the third administration than at the first for both methamphetamine-alcohol conditions (F(3,24)=15.4-26.5, p<0.0001, d=0.8-1.6), and only the larger-alcohol combination still exceeded either drug alone. Blood-pressure effects were unchanged across administrations. The first administration was in the morning and the third in the evening two nights later, after drug-disturbed sleep, which the authors name as alternatives to tolerance.

tasks.locator: Results > Tolerance > Subjective effects; Table 4
tasks.extracted: In the same study the wanted subjective effects also fell between the first and third administration: 'good drug effect' area under the curve was significantly smaller at administration 3 for both methamphetamine-alcohol conditions (F(3,24)=12.1-14.9, p<0.005, d=0.7-0.8), and for the larger-alcohol combination ratings of 'content' fell from 122.6 (SEM 40.3) to 72.6 (SEM 26.1), 'energetic' from 118.2 (SEM 31.5) to 70.1 (SEM 23.0), 'high' from 96.6 (SEM 27.0) to 56.0 (SEM 18.3) and drug liking from 3.1 (SEM 1.7) to 1.1 (SEM 1.5).

tasks.locator: Results > Acute effects (day 2) > Cardiovascular effects and > Subjective effects; Table 3
tasks.extracted: At the first administration both methamphetamine-alcohol combinations raised heart rate more than either drug alone, and the larger alcohol dose more than the smaller (F(21,168)=10.9-30.2, p<0.005); ratings of 'good drug effect' were higher under both combinations than under either drug alone (F=12.5-52.0, p<0.05), while alcohol alone produced the highest ratings of 'drunk' (peak 44.2, SEM 13.5) and 'sedated' (34.3, SEM 11.1) against 13.9 and 10.6 for the larger-alcohol combination. Breath alcohol did not differ between alcohol alone and that combination.

tasks.locator: Results > Acute effects (day 2) > Cognitive/psychomotor performance effects; Figure 3
tasks.extracted: Alcohol alone reduced maximum tracking speed on the divided-attention task compared with all other conditions (F(18,144)=6.3-12.9, p<0.05) and hits on the rapid information task compared with methamphetamine alone (F=6.7, p<0.05), while neither combination produced these decrements; the combination with the larger alcohol dose did raise errors on the repeated-acquisition task compared with methamphetamine alone and with the smaller-alcohol combination (F=14.4-18.2, p<0.001).

tasks.locator: Results > Sleep effects; Table 5, Actiwatch measures
tasks.extracted: All methamphetamine conditions reduced hours slept and sleep efficiency on the night of day 2 compared with alcohol alone (F(12,96)=11.6-30.7, p<0.005), and methamphetamine alone reduced both more than the combination with the larger alcohol dose (F=4.6, p<0.05); sleep-onset latency was 53.4 minutes (SEM 13.1) after methamphetamine alone against 20.6 (SEM 3.9) after alcohol alone, with 6.9 (SEM 0.9) against 3.5 (SEM 0.6) awakenings an hour.

tasks.locator: Results > Tolerance > Cardiovascular and BAL effects and > Subjective effects; Figure 4
tasks.extracted: By the third administration, about 36 hours after the first, the heart-rate area under the curve was significantly smaller than at the first administration for both combinations (F(3,24)=15.4-26.5, p<0.0001) and only the larger-alcohol combination still exceeded either drug alone; 'good drug effect' area was likewise smaller (F=12.1-14.9, p<0.005) and no longer differed from alcohol alone, while blood-pressure effects were unchanged across administrations.

tasks.locator: Methods and materials > Participants, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd-3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Qualifications stated by the authors: only one of the nine men used methamphetamine currently while all nine used cocaine; the concern that people might drink more or misjudge their impairment is called speculative, with no self-administration or choice measure taken; and the smaller third response could reflect the time of day (morning first, evening third) or the previous night's drug-disturbed sleep rather than tolerance. No condition tested tolerance to one drug after a course of the other.

tasks.locator: Table 2, MDMA and MDA rows; Results > Pharmacokinetics, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: A second 100 mg dose 24 hours after the first gave an area under the concentration-time curve of 2564 ng.h/mL (SD 762) against 1452 (SD 771) after the first, a ratio of 1.77 (77% higher), and a peak of 232 ng/mL (SD 39) against 180 (SD 33), a ratio of 1.29 (29% higher), both p<=0.001; the metabolite MDA rose 64% in exposure and 40% at peak. About 12 ng/mL of MDMA from the first dose was still present when the second was given.

tasks.locator: Results > Pharmacological effects, the paragraphs on physiological parameters (p. 367) and on hormones (p. 370); Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'The pharmacological effects after the second administration' (p. 373)
tasks.extracted: Effects after the second dose were slightly larger on blood pressure (peak systolic rise 34 mm Hg against 25; diastolic 20 against 10), heart rate (22 against 16 beats/min, significant only at 40 minutes) and cortisol (peak 49% higher), but unchanged on pupil diameter, the Maddox-wing measure, the amphetamine subscale and prolactin; the authors read the unchanged measures as 'the possible appearance of some degree of tolerance' and note that in no measure did effects exceed what the concentrations predicted.

tasks.locator: Table 1, HR and subjective rows (p. 887); Table 2, MDMA rows (p. 889); Results > Pharmacokinetics, 2nd paragraph (p. 889)
tasks.extracted: Taking 50 mg two hours before a 100 mg dose raised peak MDMA concentration to 311.16 ng/mL (SD 66.48) from 202.92 (SD 30.30) with 100 mg alone (p<0.001), 12.8% above dose proportionality in peak and 16.2% in exposure, with half-life unchanged (10.48 h against 10.41). Heart rate did not rise with the added dose (peak 33.05, SD 13.25, against 33.50, SD 11.87; area under the curve 69.98 against 57.75, neither significant), and none of the wanted subjective effects differed in peak or area under the curve.

tasks.locator: Table 1, SBP, DBP, T and PD rows (p. 887); Results > Physiological measures, 1st-2nd paragraphs (p. 888)
tasks.extracted: In the same study the measures that did track concentration were blood pressure (systolic area under the curve 72.96, SD 22.12, against 49.35, SD 24.28, p=0.029; diastolic 46.82, SD 27.82, against 18.81, SD 21.09, p=0.015), pupil diameter (area under the curve 11.92, SD 3.33, against 9.42, SD 1.83, p=0.037) and body temperature (differences at 2.3, 2.6 and 3 hours), none of which differed significantly at the peak.

tasks.locator: Results > Acute subjective effects, 1st paragraph; Table 1, 'Any drug effect' and 'Good drug effect' rows; Table 3, MDMA rows
tasks.extracted: A 60 mg booster two hours after 120 mg lengthened the duration of 'any drug effect' to 5.6 h (SD 1.8) from 4.6 h (SD 1.5) with the single dose (p<0.01) and raised the areas under several effect curves, while peak ratings did not differ (83, SD 21, against 85, SD 20 for 'any drug effect'; 86, SD 29, against 87, SD 19 for 'good drug effect'). Peak plasma concentration rose 1.50-fold (90% CI 1.43-1.57) and 9-hour exposure 1.47-fold (1.40-1.54), with half-life 7.2 h in both conditions.

tasks.locator: Results > Autonomic effects; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Blood pressure, heart rate, rate-pressure product and body temperature rose under both MDMA conditions against placebo and lasted longer after the booster without a higher maximum; the authors attribute the unchanged maxima despite higher concentrations to acute pharmacodynamic tolerance, noting that effects subsided within the 9-hour session while the mean concentration at discharge after the booster exceeded the mean peak after the single dose. The numerical autonomic values are in a supplement that the first reader did not open.

tasks.locator: Results > Participants and blinding, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, Emax rows
tasks.extracted: Qualifications: blinding largely failed (every participant identified placebo correctly and 76% of MDMA sessions were identified correctly immediately afterwards), and the peak ratings against which the absence of an increase is measured were already 83-87 out of 100, so a ceiling on the scales cannot be separated from tolerance for the subjective measures.

tasks.locator: The paragraph beginning 'The pharmacodynamic effects of single doses of MDMA' and the one following it (left column); Subjective reports of tolerance and diminishing responsiveness to MDMA, 2nd-3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The review states that no laboratory study has given a series of MDMA doses to humans and that chronic tolerance therefore cannot be investigated in humans under double-blind, placebo-controlled conditions, so all human evidence comes from surveys of people who use ecstasy recreationally; in those surveys 58% of 1151 people reported tolerance and about 85-95% of 430 people using it regularly reported declining subjective efficacy, with an earlier survey finding 67% of those with six or more occasions reporting that positive effects decreased and negative effects increased.

tasks.locator: Dosage escalation in recreational Ecstasy users, 1st-2nd paragraphs; Table 1; Table 2
tasks.extracted: Reported dose rises with past use: 1.8 tablets a session currently against 1.2 when starting in 430 people; usual dose 1.8 (SD 0.9), 2.2 (SD 1.1) and 3.7 (SD 3.8) tablets and maximum ever 3.6 (SD 1.5), 5.1 (SD 2.0) and 10.9 (SD 8.7) across lifetime-use groups of 14, 14 and 11 people, with the maximum significant at p<0.01 and the usual dose only at p<0.10; and a usual dose of 1-2 tablets reported by 100% of 109, 84% of 136 and 62% of 37 people in novice, moderate and heaviest groups, with a maximum of ten or more tablets in a week reported by 0%, 9% and 35% (chi-square 39.40 and 169.99, df 4, p<0.001).

tasks.locator: The paragraph beginning 'A related problem is the issue of dosage' (p. 72); Dosage escalation in recreational Ecstasy users, last paragraph (p. 75); Table 3 (p. 78)
tasks.extracted: Qualifications reported in the same review: one study found no dose escalation with longer use (2.1 tablets per occasion after 10.9 years against 2.5 after 3.9 years, not significant); average MDMA content per tablet in United Kingdom forensic samples fell about 20% across the mid-1990s (102 to 88 mg, then 75 to 73 mg) so falling tablet strength cannot be excluded for studies from that period; and in the same internet sample, problems attributed to ecstasy rose with lifetime use (depression 33%, 54% and 65%; memory problems 19%, 52% and 73%), so heavier use goes with more reported harm as well as with larger doses.

tasks.locator: Results > Pharmacological effects, the paragraph beginning 'In reference to physiological parameters' (right column)
tasks.extracted: Criteria for isolated systolic hypertension (above 140 mm Hg) were met by 6 of 9 men after the first 100 mg dose and by 8 of 9 after the second dose 24 hours later, with episodes lasting a mean of 1 h (range 0.5-2) and 1.4 h (range 0.5-3); two men met criteria for sinus tachycardia (above 100 beats/min), both after the second dose, lasting 15-30 minutes. Peak rises were 34 mm Hg systolic and 20 diastolic after the second dose against 25 and 10 after the first.

tasks.locator: Table 1, SBP and DBP rows (p. 887); Results > Physiological measures, 1st paragraph (p. 888)
tasks.extracted: With 50 mg two hours before 100 mg, every one of the ten men exceeded 140/90 mm Hg; the systolic area under the curve over the 2-6 hour window was 72.96 (SD 22.12) against 49.35 (SD 24.28) for 100 mg alone (p=0.029) and the diastolic 46.82 (SD 27.82) against 18.81 (SD 21.09) (p=0.015), while heart rate did not differ in peak or area under the curve.

tasks.locator: Results > Autonomic effects; Table 2, List of complaints rows; Results > Acute and subacute adverse effects, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: With a 60 mg booster two hours after 120 mg, blood pressure, heart rate, rate-pressure product and temperature lasted longer than with the single dose but did not reach higher maxima, and no participant exceeded 180 mm Hg systolic or 40 degrees Celsius. Acute complaint scores did not differ significantly between booster and single dose (22, SD 15, against 20, SD 13), although two of 25 participants, both women receiving the booster as their first MDMA experience, left the study after headache and nausea followed by weeks of anxiety and restlessness, and are excluded from that comparison.

tasks.locator: Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'The changes seen in the concentrations between first and second doses'
tasks.extracted: The authors note that acute MDMA toxicity has been linked to high plasma concentrations and doses, that cardiovascular complications were more frequent after the second dose in their study, and that with further doses the contribution of each previous dose would grow because MDMA inhibits its own metabolism; they present this as speculation about what would happen beyond two doses, which was not tested.

tasks.locator: Results › Unadjusted rates of death from drug overdose, 1st paragraph; Table 2, benzodiazepine prescription history and daily dose rows
tasks.extracted: Of 2,400 overdose deaths, 1,185 (49%) occurred during current benzodiazepine prescription. Unadjusted overdose death rates per 100,000 person-years (estimates for the source population): none 71 (95% CI 66–76; 794 deaths), former 187 (170–205; 421 deaths), current 316 (298–334; 1,185 deaths); by prescribed daily benzodiazepine dose, >0–10 mg 152, >10–20 mg 301, >20–30 mg 518, >30–40 mg 600, >40 mg 805 (689–930). Editors' calculation: current against none, a difference of 245 per 100,000 person-years. The 0 mg/day row of Table 2 is internally inconsistent and is not used.

tasks.locator: Results › Adjusted analyses, 1st paragraph; Table 3, Models 1 and 2
tasks.extracted: Adjusted for sex, age, race, ethnicity, area poverty, time-varying opioid dose, recent substance-use admissions, Charlson index, diagnoses of substance use disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, other anxiety disorder, depression, bipolar or psychotic disorder and cancer, and other drug use: hazard ratio for overdose death 3.86 (3.49–4.26) for current and 2.33 (2.05–2.64) for former benzodiazepine receipt against none. Within current receipt, against >0–10 mg/day: 1.69 (1.42–2.01), 2.34 (1.91–2.86), 2.65 (2.10–3.33) and 3.06 (2.38–3.92) for >10–20, >20–30, >30–40 and >40 mg/day; temazepam against clonazepam 0.63 (0.48–0.82); dosing schedule not associated.

tasks.locator: Results › Adjusted analyses, 1st paragraph; Table 4
tasks.extracted: The interaction between benzodiazepine history and opioid dose was not significant (P = 0.60), which the authors describe as relations neither greater nor less than additive; in a Cox model this tests departure from multiplicative hazards (study card, reporting issue 1). Hazard ratios for ≥100 against >0–<20 mg morphine-equivalent per day: no benzodiazepine 3.30 (2.62–4.16), former 3.00 (2.19–4.11), current 3.92 (3.17–4.85).

tasks.locator: Methods › Study design and population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Deaths from drug overdose, 1st paragraph; Drug prescribing patterns, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Results › Sample, 1st paragraph; Table 1
tasks.extracted: Case-cohort within VHA patients receiving outpatient opioid analgesics in financial years 2004–2009: 2,400 overdose deaths and 420,386 random controls (5% annual samples), 422,786 analysed after excluding methadone maintenance (221) and palliative or hospice care (5,816). Outcome: any intentional, unintentional or undetermined poisoning death by any drug (National Death Index). Exposure: person-days classified as current, former or no benzodiazepine receipt from fills and days' supply, doses computed as prescribed. 112,069 (27%) filled a benzodiazepine; they had more anxiety disorders (20% against 5%), post-traumatic stress disorder (22% against 9%), depression (38% against 19%) and substance use disorders (13% against 10%).

tasks.locator: Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses of study, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Findings in context, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The authors note veterans, mostly men; non-VHA prescriptions unseen; doses assume drugs were taken as prescribed; indications unknown. They say benzodiazepines go more often to people with substance misuse and psychiatric disorders, that residual confounding by their severity may remain, that the raised risk after prescriptions ended may reflect these conditions or continued illicit, outside or leftover benzodiazepines, and that half the deaths occurred without a benzodiazepine prescription.
tasks.quote: might be better conceptualized as a marker of risk

tasks.locator: Abstract (Results); Results, 4th paragraph; Fig 3 legend
tasks.extracted: Adjusted annual incidence of an emergency-room visit or inpatient admission for opioid overdose: 1.16% (95% CI 1.13–1.18) without and 2.42% (2.32–2.51) with concurrent benzodiazepine use, odds ratio 2.14 (2.05–2.24); intermittent opioid prescriptions 1.02% against 1.45%, OR 1.42 (1.33–1.51); chronic opioid prescriptions 3.13% against 5.36%, OR 1.81 (1.67–1.96); adjusted for year, sex, age, the Table 1 comorbidities and prior health spending, with standard errors clustered by person.

tasks.locator: Methods › Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Variables, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Analyses, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: MarketScan claims, 2001–2013: 315,428 privately insured people aged 18–64, continuously enrolled for 13 years, without cancer, who filled an opioid prescription. Concurrent use: at least one day of overlap between opioid and benzodiazepine prescription intervals in a calendar year. Outcome: emergency-room visit or admission with codes for opioid poisoning or a potential opioid adverse event plus an opioid overdose code, during an opioid prescription interval or within 7 days. Covariates: age, sex, year, comorbidities and prior spending; opioid dose is not among them. Chronic opioid prescription: more than 10 prescriptions or more than 120 days' supply in a year.

tasks.locator: Results, 7th and 8th paragraphs; Discussion › Strengths and limitations of this study, 1st, 3rd and 5th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: In a broader sample of 3,810,747 people enrolled for at least 2 years, adjusted relative risks were 1.66 (1.64–1.69) for intermittent and 1.61 (1.58–1.63) for chronic opioid prescriptions. A residual-confounding analysis assumed a binary confounder in 75% of exposed and 0% of unexposed person-years. The authors state that unobserved confounding cannot be excluded, that only hospital-treated events in people who survived were counted, and that heroin and illegally bought prescription drugs are not captured.

tasks.locator: Abstract (Results); Results › Trends in Alcohol and Benzodiazepine Co-involvement, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Figure 1 (image)
tasks.extracted: Of 399,230 US opioid-involved poisoning deaths in 1999–2017, the share whose death certificates also named benzodiazepines rose from 8.7% in 1999 to 26.2% in 2010 and fell to 21.0% in 2017; death rates for opioid overdoses involving benzodiazepines rose 10.3-fold, against 5.0-fold for all opioid overdose deaths. By subtype: heroin 4.0% (1999) to 17.1% (2017); methadone 15.6% (2000) to 32.0% (2017); prescription opioids 15.6% (2000) to 33.1% (2017); synthetic opioids between 15.0% and 25.9%.

tasks.locator: Results › Current Co-involvement in 2015-2017 by Opioid Subtype, Sex, and State, 1st–3rd paragraphs; Table
tasks.extracted: 2015–2017: 26,728 of 122,940 opioid overdose deaths (21.7%) named benzodiazepines; men 15,837 of 82,506 (19.2%), women 10,891 of 40,434 (26.9%); heroin 6,972 of 43,940 (15.9%); methadone 3,202 of 9,868 (32.4%); prescription opioids 13,905 of 41,709 (33.3%); synthetic opioids 9,978 of 57,459 (17.4%); by state from 5.4% (Delaware) to 45.5% (Arkansas), median 22.0%.

tasks.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 6th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Death certificates misclassify and omit drugs: about 20% of drug poisoning deaths in 2011 and 12% in 2017 named no specific drug, and states named at least one drug in 54.7% to 99.3% of deaths in 2017; medical-examiner guidance from 2013 recommends benzodiazepine testing; the database has no individual-level data, so deaths involving opioids, benzodiazepines and alcohol together cannot be counted. The authors note two toxicology studies with benzodiazepines in 60% of opioid deaths, which they call inconsistent with their data.

tasks.locator: Abstract (Results); Results › Unadjusted rates of death from drug overdose, 1st paragraph; Table 2
tasks.extracted: Of 2,400 US veterans who died of a drug overdose (any drug, any intent) while receiving VHA opioid analgesics in 2004–2009, 1,185 (49%) died during a period of concurrent benzodiazepine prescription, 421 after a benzodiazepine prescription had ended and 794 with none.

tasks.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, past medication use (120 days), benzodiazepines row
tasks.extracted: Among Ontario public-drug-plan opioid recipients, 971 of 1,256 people who died an accidental, coroner-confirmed opioid-related death (77.3%) and 2,604 of 4,619 matched controls (56.4%) had a benzodiazepine dispensed in the 120 days before the index date (standardized difference 0.46); this is a descriptive comparison after matching, and no adjusted estimate for benzodiazepines is reported.

tasks.locator: Abstract (Results); Results › Trends in Alcohol and Benzodiazepine Co-involvement, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figures 1 and 2 (images)
tasks.extracted: Alcohol co-involvement in all US opioid overdose deaths rose from 12.4% in 1999 to 14.7% in 2017 and stayed near 15% from 2008; death rates for alcohol-involved opioid overdoses rose 5.5-fold from 1999 to 2017 (all opioid overdose deaths 5.0-fold). By subtype: heroin 10.3%–20.1% over the period and 15.5% in 2017 (0.7 deaths per 100,000); synthetic opioids 11.5% in 2013 to 14.9% in 2017 (1.3 per 100,000); prescription opioids 14.3%–15.4% in 2007–2017 (0.7 per 100,000 in 2017); methadone below 10% until 2017 (0.1 per 100,000).

tasks.locator: Results › Current Co-involvement in 2015-2017 by Opioid Subtype, Sex, and State, 1st–3rd paragraphs; Table
tasks.extracted: 2015–2017: alcohol named in 18,419 of 122,940 opioid overdose deaths (15.0%); men 17.2%, women 10.5%; heroin 16.5%, methadone 10.0%, prescription opioids 14.2%, synthetic opioids 14.9% (8,584 of 57,459); by state from 7.4% (Mississippi) to 28.7% (District of Columbia), median 13.3%; state alcohol and benzodiazepine shares uncorrelated (r = 0.08).

tasks.locator: Methods › Data Source, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Co-involvement is the mention of alcohol (T51.0 or T51.9) among the multiple causes on certificates of drug poisoning deaths with an opioid code. The authors state that alcohol is under-reported and often excluded from drug-related deaths, that the 2013 medical-examiner guidance does not address alcohol testing, that the 2006–2007 change in alcohol co-involvement may reflect 8 more states reporting and 481 extra alcohol-involved deaths reported by 8 others, that 12% of drug poisoning deaths in 2017 named no drug, that no individual-level data or blood levels were available, and that the counts are likely underestimated.

tasks.locator: Results › Association of Co-involvement With State-Level Binge Drinking and Benzodiazepine Prescribing, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 legend; Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Across states, self-reported binge-drinking prevalence (BRFSS) correlated with the alcohol share of opioid overdose deaths in 2015–2017, r = 0.34 (P = .02); South Dakota excluded for too few deaths. The authors state that the state-level correlations are not causal and may be prone to observational biases.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph; Conclusions, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors report, from studies not read here, higher alcohol co-involvement with toxicology data: 22.3% of opioid deaths in Ontario, Canada (Gomes et al., 2017) and 18% alcohol-only co-intoxication in Massachusetts (Barocas et al., 2019); second-hand figures, cited only to show that certificate-based shares are lower.
tasks.quote: Alcohol remains an important and underrecognized cointoxicant in overdose deaths.

tasks.locator: Methods › Setting, 1st paragraph; Data sources, 1st paragraph; Identification of patients and outcomes, 1st–3rd paragraphs; Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
tasks.extracted: Ontario Public Drug Programs (people aged 65 or over, unemployed, on disability benefits, with high drug costs relative to income, in home care or long-term care), 1997–2013; opioid recipients aged 15–105 without cancer or recent palliative care. Cases: coroner-confirmed opioid-related deaths (autopsy and toxicology), suicides and homicides excluded; 1,256 of 1,391 eligible cases matched by incidence density sampling to 4,619 controls on a disease risk index, age, sex, year and kidney disease. 94.5% of cases and 94.2% of controls were under 65; 42.1% and 43.8% in the lowest income fifth; 24 cases (1.9%) also had heroin on toxicology.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st and 4th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The authors read the result as a drug–drug interaction and list limitations: a low-income public-plan population, mostly under 65; only government-reimbursed retail prescriptions; adherence and cash or illicit purchases unknown; the indication for gabapentin unknown; confounding by indication possible, which they argue against from the risk-index matching, opioid-dose adjustment, adjustment for severity markers and the NSAID result.
tasks.quote: support the existence of a life-threatening drug–drug interaction

tasks.locator: Abstract (Methods and findings); Results › Z-drugs and gabapentinoids, 1st paragraph; Table 4, gabapentinoid rows
tasks.extracted: In 12,118 people in methadone or buprenorphine treatment in UK primary care, gabapentinoid co-prescription: drug-poisoning deaths 5 in 538 person-years (0.93 per 100) against 108 in 19,410 (0.56), adjusted HR 1.54 (0.60–3.98), p = 0.373; all-cause deaths 83 in 998 person-years (8.32 per 100) against 574 in 35,129 (1.63), adjusted HR 1.71 (1.33–2.20); other deaths 46 in 571 (8.06 per 100) against 239 in 19,815 (1.21), adjusted HR 1.83 (1.28–2.62); no dose analysis possible; the authors call these analyses underpowered.

tasks.locator: Abstract (Methods and findings); Results › Associations of co-prescription with mortality › Benzodiazepines, 1st paragraph; Table 4, DRP rows
tasks.extracted: Drug-related poisoning deaths by benzodiazepine co-prescription (during OAT or up to 12 months after): off 74 deaths in 16,270 person-years (0.45 per 100), on 39 in 3,679 (1.06); unadjusted HR 2.35 (1.59–3.47), adjusted HR 2.96 (1.97–4.43), p < 0.001; normal dose 25 in 2,889 (0.87), adjusted HR 2.51 (1.57–4.01); high dose (above the British National Formulary maximum) 14 in 790 (1.77), 4.57 (2.46–8.47); linear effect of dose 2.22 (1.69–2.92). Adjusted for sex, year, comorbidity, region, OAT type, OAT period and other sedatives.

tasks.locator: Results › Interactions between benzodiazepine co-prescription and OAT period, 1st paragraph; Table 5
tasks.extracted: Drug-related poisoning deaths with and without benzodiazepine co-prescription: on OAT 20 deaths in 2,914 person-years (0.69 per 100) against 24 in 10,091 (0.24), adjusted HR 2.92 (1.60–5.33); off OAT, up to a year after, 19 in 764 (2.49) against 50 in 6,179 (0.81), adjusted HR 2.92 (1.70–5.02); no interaction with treatment period.

tasks.locator: Abstract (Methods and findings); Results › Z-drugs and gabapentinoids, 1st paragraph; Table 4, z-drug rows
tasks.extracted: Z-drug co-prescription: drug-related poisoning 15 deaths in 1,110 person-years (1.35 per 100) against 98 in 18,838 (0.52), adjusted HR 2.75 (1.57–4.83); normal dose (10 deaths) 3.66 (1.86–7.19), high dose (5 deaths) 1.55 (0.59–4.06), no dose gradient; all-cause 1.26 (0.94–1.69); other deaths 0.79 (0.49–1.28).

tasks.locator: Table 4, all-cause and non-DRP benzodiazepine rows; Results › Overall association of concurrent prescription with mortality risk, 1st paragraph; Table 6
tasks.extracted: Benzodiazepine co-prescription and all-cause deaths: 144 in 7,361 person-years (1.96 per 100) against 513 in 28,766 (1.78), adjusted HR 1.17 (0.97–1.42); other deaths 0.91 (0.66–1.25). Concurrent prescription during OAT against none (Table 6), adjusted: benzodiazepine drug-related poisoning 3.34 (2.14–5.20; unadjusted 1.98), all-cause 1.87 (1.55–2.25; unadjusted 1.22), other deaths 1.73 (1.28–2.33; unadjusted 1.10); z-drug drug-related poisoning 1.64 (1.02–2.64), all-cause 1.37 (1.09–1.72), other 1.37 (0.95–1.96).

tasks.locator: Results › Association of concurrent prescription of benzodiazepines, z-drugs, and gabapentinoids with duration of OAT episodes, 1st paragraph; Table 2
tasks.extracted: Of 27,598 analysed OAT episodes, 7,961 had concurrent benzodiazepine prescription. Adjusted mean episode duration: none 244 days (236–252), concurrent benzodiazepine 416 (404–429), z-drug 441 (421–461); methadone episodes 286 (275–297) without and 466 (450–483) with a benzodiazepine; buprenorphine 135 (126–144) and 234 (217–250).

tasks.locator: Methods › OAT patients, 1st paragraph; OAT episodes, 1st paragraph; Confounding factors, 1st paragraph; Deaths, 1st paragraph; Results › Study participants, 1st paragraph; Table 1
tasks.extracted: CPRD primary-care records, 1998–2014: 12,118 patients aged 15–64 prescribed methadone or buprenorphine for opioid dependence (prescriptions for pain and doses below the minimum expected for treatment excluded); follow-up on treatment and up to 1 year after; adjustment for sex, age, year, a comorbidity index of 17 chronic illnesses, region, treatment type and period, and the other sedatives; cause of death from ONS for the linked English subset (7,106 patients; 113 drug-related poisoning deaths, 87.6% men). Concurrent benzodiazepine prescription: 42.2% of all patients and 61.9% of those who died of drug poisoning.

tasks.locator: Discussion › Principal findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion › Strengths and limitations of this study, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors describe a threefold increase in drug-related poisoning mortality with benzodiazepines, during and after treatment, and higher at doses above the formulary maximum; they acknowledge confounding by indication, that propensity scores added little in their earlier work, that no instrument was available and that non-prescribed sedatives could not be measured, and still call their result the strongest evidence that benzodiazepine co-prescription is itself a cause of drug-poisoning death.
